item.subject: chemistry
item.subtopic_label: Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)
item.stem: Which compound contains two different elements with identical oxidation states?
item.stem_lead: Which compound contains two different elements with identical oxidation states?

learn_by_solve.solve: HClO (HOCl): H is +1, O is −2, so Cl is +1. Hydrogen and chlorine are two different elements with the same oxidation state. Mg(OH)₂ is Mg +2, O −2, H +1 — three different states; two OH groups are the same elements repeated, not two different elements sharing a state. Na₂SO₄ is Na +1, S +6, O −2. NH₄Cl is N −3, H +1, Cl −1. Only HClO has a matching pair.

B.pathway: Student reads (OH)₂ as ‘two elements with the same oxidation state’: two hydroxide units are the same two elements repeated, and in OH oxygen is −2 while hydrogen is +1.

followup.stem: Mg(OH)₂ has two hydroxide groups. In each OH, what are the oxidation states of O and H?

options.A: Both −1, so two different elements share the same state
options.B: O is −2 and H is +1, so O and H do not share a state
options.D: O is −1 and H is −1 because OH is the hydroxide ion

followup.why: Hydroxide is O −2 and H +1. Repeating OH twice does not create two different elements with the same oxidation state. Magnesium is +2, which matches neither.

C.pathway: Student does not complete 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 for Na₂SO₄, so they never see Na +1, S +6, O −2 as three different states (or they use sulfite S +4).

followup.stem: In Na₂SO₄, Na is +1 and O is −2. What is the oxidation state of S?
followup.why: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 gives S = +6. The three elements are +1, +6 and −2. No two different elements share a state. Two sodium atoms are the same element.

D.pathway: Student assigns Cl in NH₄Cl as +1 (as in HCl or HClO) so that H +1 and Cl +1 look like a matching pair. Chlorine here is chloride, Cl −1.

followup.stem: What is the oxidation state of chlorine in NH₄Cl?
followup.why: NH₄Cl is ammonium chloride: Cl is −1. Nitrogen in NH₄⁺ is −3 and hydrogen is +1. None of N, H and Cl share an oxidation state. Cl +1 is the HClO assignment, not this salt.

modify_seeds.label: If B · two OH groups as ‘two elements’
modify_seeds.instruction: Rewrite this oxidation-state item so option B remains the trap for a student who treats two repeated hydroxide groups as two different elements with the same oxidation state. Keep a compound in which O is −2 and H is +1. Rewrite the stem and all four options as one coherent item. Do not print mix-up labels. Recalculate the key.

modify_seeds.label: If C · sulfur OS in sulfate
modify_seeds.instruction: Rewrite this oxidation-state item so option C remains the trap for a student who assigns sulfur in a sulfate as +4 (sulfite) or who drops the factor of four oxygens in 2(+1)+S+4(−2)=0. Keep a sulfate whose elements are +1, +6 and −2. Rewrite the stem and all four options as one coherent item. Do not print mix-up labels. Recalculate the key.

modify_seeds.label: If D · Cl in chloride vs HClO
modify_seeds.instruction: Rewrite this oxidation-state item so option D remains the trap for a student who gives chlorine in an ammonium halide the oxidation state +1 (as in HClO) instead of −1 as chloride. Keep N −3, H +1, Cl −1 on the trap compound. Rewrite the stem and all four options as one coherent item. Do not print mix-up labels. Recalculate the key.
